newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices rise as U.S. petrol stocks show deficit.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rise as U.S. petrol stocks show deficit.

text.p: Oil prices perked up on Wednesday after weekly data released overnight showed a fall in United States' gasoline (petrol) stocks, traders said.
North Sea Brent Blend crude, the international benchmark, was 16 cents up at $19.61 a barrel by 1637 GMT on the London futures market.
"A lot of people were short...and the APIs helped swing a few fence-sitters off the fence," said Charles Gray, energy analyst at Prudential Bache in London.

American Petroleum Institute (API) data showed a fall of 3.2 million barrels in gasoline stocks last week, when traders had expected stocks to be unchanged or up by one million barrels in the approach to the U.S. driving season.
The gasoline draw put stocks down 7.3 million barrels from year-ago levels.
Oil inventory for the same week reported by the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) on Wednesday echoed the APIs with a gasoline draw of 3.8 million barrels.

But trade on Wednesday was volatile with the bearish tone that has knocked 20 percent off the value of a barrel of crude oil in the last six weeks appearing to grapple with the more bullish stock data.
Brent hit a high of $19.84 earlier on Wednesday before briefly touching a trough of $19.30.
The benchmark crude had hit a low of $19.09 on Monday and is still almost $5 below the high seen in January.

A study by the London-based think-tank the Centre for Global Energy Studies (CGES) said world oil prices were expected to remain week for the rest of the decade as rising supply outpaced demand growth.

Assuming a substantial increase in production capacity within the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), continuing growth in non-OPEC output until the year 2001 and the full lifting of sanctions against Iraq from 1999 onwards, the CGES expected prices to decline for four or five years.
"It seems that non-OPEC output holds the key to future oil prices, for when it stops growing we find that real oil prices start to rise," the CGES said.
The report said price weakness was because potential supply would rise by more than the 6.9 million barrels per day (bpd) jump in demand.

Non-OPEC output is expected to rise by 3.4 million bpd between 1996 and 2001 while Iraq should be producing at capacity from 1999 onwards, which would bring another 2.5 million bpd into play within two years.
A mild winter in the northern hemisphere and rising Iraqi oil sales have combined to force prices down this year.
